query: Consider the following context: Constituent phases and their corresponding phase transformations are important in developing alloys. In that context, which method can be used for control of phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A stepwise thermo‐mechanical treatment—employing sequential high‐temperature homogenization, controlled deformation (rolling), and staged aging—is effective in steering phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs by promoting the formation of coherent nanoprecipitates that strengthen the alloy without excessively compromising ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: Homogenized or as-cast Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloy with a largely single‐phase matrix.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled, stepwise thermo-mechanical processing route that includes: (1) high-temperature homogenization, (2) deformation processing (combination of hot and cold rolling), and (3) sequential aging treatments at different temperatures.
generation.conditions: Processing in an inert atmosphere with defined temperature steps (inspired by the refractory HEA study, e.g., an intermediate anneal followed by aging at a lower temperature) and specific deformation reductions. Processing parameters must be tailored to the Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy to induce fine, coherent precipitates.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of coherent nanoprecipitates (analogous to δ-lamellae and γ″ particles in the refractory HEA study) within the alloy matrix that interact with dislocations.
generation.mechanism: The coherent precipitates provide sites that hinder dislocation motion by either pinning or moderate shearing, thus enhancing yield strength while maintaining ductility through an optimized balance of precipitation hardening and stress relief.
generation.predicted_outcome: The processed alloy will exhibit a significantly higher yield and ultimate tensile strength compared to alloys processed by traditional single-step aging, while retaining or even improving ductility due to the controlled, coherent precipitate structure.
generation.baseline: Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA processed through conventional thermal treatments without the stepwise processing regime.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis assumes that the phase stability and nucleation kinetics in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs are sufficiently similar to those in the refractory HEA system, though adjustments in aging temperatures and deformation schedules may be necessary.
generation.uncertainty: The exact nature and identities of the precipitates in the Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni system under these processing conditions are uncertain, as are the precise processing parameters required to achieve the desired microstructural evolution.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare samples of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA. Process one set using the proposed stepwise thermo-mechanical treatment (high-temperature homogenization, subsequent deformation (rolling), followed by sequential aging) and a control set using a conventional, single-step aging route. Use transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) to characterize the microstructure and precipitate coherence. Perform standard uniaxial tensile tests to assess mechanical properties.
measurements: Precipitate morphology, size, distribution, and coherence via TEM/SEM.
Phase composition via X-ray diffraction and EBSD.
Mechanical properties: yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility from tensile tests.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the stepwise thermo-mechanical processed samples do not exhibit a distinct formation of coherent nanoprecipitates or show no significant improvement in strength and ductility compared to the control samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.
